About the Cover
Mindanawon life is a colorful depiction of Filipino culture and progress, regardless of 
eligion, race, or geographic orientation.
This year’s cover design pays homage to this diversity.
You will see distinct facets in the everyday lives of the Mindanawon: their livelihoods 
and the goods they produce, crafts representing their heritage, and the festivals 
they celebrate. We feature Davao’s famous icons such as the Philippine eagle, 
walingwaling, and durian; the famous tuna from General Santos City; the vintas from 
the Regatta de Zamboanga, the highlight of the yearly Hermosa Festival; Cagayan 
de Oro’s motorela; the St. Augustine Cathedral where the giant Oro fish is said to live 
underneath, according to local lore; and the iconic Sulu Provincial Capitol, considered 
one of the most beautiful capitol buildings in the country with its golden domes and 
Moorish-inspired architectural design.
Mindanao is also home to vibrant prints. The first illustration portrayed in the connected 
circles depicts the silk and cotton Inaul fabric from the people of Maguindanao. 
We also feature the Yakan fabric (third illustration) made by the Yakan people from 
Basilan and the Zamboanga Peninsula; as well as T’nalak, an abaca fabric woven 
by the T’boli women (eighth illustration). Its design comes to the weaver through a 
dream, thus earning South Cotabato the nickname “Land of the Dreamweavers”.  
Geometric and flowing patterns inspired by the okir motif, which decorate the 
background and top and bottom borders of the cover, depict the indigenous artistry 
and skill of the Maranaos.
Distinct yet interconnected, the points are linked to each other through lines that 
form the shape of a traditional telephone receiver, representing correspondence and 
communication among the diverse peoples and institutions of Mindanao.
Its varied people, vivid culture, and splendid natural beauty altogether make up the 
unique wonder that is Mindanao—truly the Philippines’ land of promise.
Note from the Publisher
This Government Directory is not for sale.
The contents of this publication, including the names, positions, and contact details 
of the government officials, are based on data available as of December 1, 2024 as 
validated by the agencies. However, some information may still change before the 
actual printing date as determined by the submission and/or notice of the concerned 
agencies.

--- PAGE 6 ---
EXECUTIVE BRANCH
The Executive Branch implements national policies and performs the executive 
and administrative functions of the National Government. The Constitution 
vests the executive power in the President of the Philippines. The President is 
assisted by the Vice President and the Members of the Cabinet in the discharge 
of executive functions. Also part of the Executive Branch are State Universities 
and Colleges and Government-Owned and/or -Controlled Corporations.

CONSTITUTIONAL 
OFFICES
CONSTITUTIONAL
OFFICES
--- PAGE 114 ---
CONSTITUTIONAL OFFICES
The 1987 Constitution of the Philippines provides for the creation of offices 
that are independent and autonomous, and whose mandates and functions 
are defined by the Constitution itself.
These Constitutional Offices are the following:
Civil Service Commission (CSC), which is the central personnel agency of 
the government
Commission on Elections (COMELEC), tasked to enforce and administer
all laws and regulations relative to the conduct of elections, plebiscites,
initiatives, referanda and recall
Commission on Audit (COA), whose primary duty is to examine, audit and
settle all accounts pertaining to the revenue and receipts of, and expenditures
or uses of funds and property owned or held in trust by the Government or 
any of its subdivisions, agencies or instrumentalities.
The following are also considered constitutionally mandated bodies:
Commission on Human Rights (CHR), with the primary function of
investigating all forms of human rights violations involving civil and
political rights
Office of the Ombudsman, which has the power to investigate on its own 
or upon complaint, any act or omission of any public official, employee, 
office or agency deemed to be illegal, unjust, improper or inefficient.

GOCCs AND

GOCCs AND

--- PAGE 128 ---
GOVERNMENT-OWNED AND/OR -CONTROLLED CORPORATIONS
Government-owned and/or -controlled corporations (GOCCs), as defined 
by Presidential Decree No. 2029 (February 1986) and Memorandum Order 
No. 64 (1993), are agencies organized as stock or non-stock corporations, 
vested with functions relating to public needs, whether governmental or
proprietary in nature, and owned by the Government of the Philippines
directly or through its instrumentalities. Established to engage in either
commercial or non-commercial activities, such agencies may be wholly-owned
by the government or, in the case of stock corporations, the government has 
direct or indirect ownership of the majority of its capital stock. Some GOCCs 
have been created by special laws and most have their own charter defining 
their governance and responsibilities.
By virtue of R.A. No. 10149 (GOCC Governance Act of 2011), GOCCs,
except for the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, state universities and colleges, 
cooperatives, local water districts, economic zone authorities and research 
institutions, are monitored by the Governance Commission for GOCCs
(GCG). The GCG serves as the central advisory and oversight body to
determine the relevence and evaluate the performance of these
corporations. It also has the power and function to ascertain whether or not 
they should be reorganized, merged, streamlined, abolished, or privatized.
STATE UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES
State universities and colleges (SUCs) are public higher education institutions
that have been created or organized by an act of Congress.
For AY 2021-2022, the Commission on Higher Education lists a total of 114 SUCs, 
with 432 satellite campuses.
Note: Data taken from CHED official website.

--- PAGE 156 ---
LEGISLATIVE BRANCH
As provided for by the Constitution, the Congress of the Philippines is the
bicameral legislative body of the Philippine Government which has the power
to enact laws, including the General Appropriations Act. In addition to 
its legislative mandate, the Congress also performs functions such as the 
confirmation of Presidential appointments,impeachment, declaration of the 
existence of a state of war and concurrence or confirmation of the amnesty 
granted by the President.
The Congress is divided into two chambers: the Senate and the House of 
Representatives.
The Senate consists of 24 duly elected Senators, 12 of whom are replaced or 
re-elected every three years, to ensure continuity of policies, as well as the 
availability of experienced members who can help and train newcomers in 
the discharge of duties.
The House of Representatives of the 19th Congress is composed of 252 
Geographical District Representatives and 63 Sectoral Representatives. The Sectoral 
Representatives constitute about 20 percent of the total number of the Members of 
the House. Each Representative serves for a term of three (3) years, and can be re-
elected for two (2) additional consecutive terms.

JUDICIAL

JUDICIAL
BRANCH
--- PAGE 180 ---
JUDICIAL BRANCH
The Constitution vests judicial power in the Supreme Court and in such lower 
courts as may be established by law.
At present, these lower courts are the Court of Appeals, Trial Courts
(Regional, Metropolitan, Municipal and Municipal  Circuit Trial Courts),
Special Courts (Sandiganbayan and Court of Tax Appeals), and Shari’a 
Courts (Shari’a District and Circuit Courts). The Supreme Court exercises 
administrative supervision over all courts and their personnel.
As provided for by the Constitution, judicial power includes the duty of the 
courts of justice to settle actual controversies involving legally demandable 
and enforceable rights, and to determine whether or not there has been a 
grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction on the 
part of any branch or instrumentality of the Government.
--- PAGE 181 ---
PB 177
ALEXANDER G. GESMUNDO

LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNITS
Local Government Units (LGUs) serve as partners of the National Government
in advancing the country’s development agenda. They are both political 
and corporate bodies, endowed with powers to manage local affairs and
promote the welfare of the people within their respective territorial
jurisdictions. The Philippines has 82 provinces, 148 cities, 1,486 municipalities, and 
42,027 barangays.*
The heads of LGUs are elected by their constituents and , except for barangay 
officials, serve for a term of three (3) years. They may be re-elected for two (2)
additional consecutive terms.
* Taken from the website of the Department of the Interior and Local Government as of March 31, 2023.

DIPLOMATIC OFFICES AND
INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS
--- PAGE 268 ---
DIPLOMATIC OFFICES
The Philippine government has welcomed 207 diplomatic and consular missions to 
the country.
Metro Manila hosts most of these embassies, which conduct a full range of 
diplomatic activities and services, including the development of commercial, 
economic, cultural and scientific relations between the Philippines and their 
respective home countries, and the issuance of passports, travel documents, 
and visas. Some consular missions are located outside of Metro Manila, but 
still in key cities of the archipelago, primarily to facilitate the delivery of 
services to their citizens, as well as to Filipinos.
There are resident and non-resident missions. The former have embassies 
or chanceries, with the respective head of mission located in the Philippines. 
The latter, on the other hand, have missions based outside the country.
The premier diplomatic mission in the Philippines is that of the Holy See, the 
Apostolic Nunciature. Its head, the Apostolic Nuncio, is by tradition the Dean 
of the Diplomatic Corps.
INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS
International organizations that have established offices in the Philippines 
are focused on various functions and issues, depending on their mandates. 
These include information and monitoring of global trends, delivery of
services such as health, social action and humanitarian aid, providing venues
for economic and political discourse, and settling of disputes. While most 
of these organizations have their primary headquarters in Metro Manila, 
a number of them have regional offices to provide better access to their
stakeholders and clients.
